note: Per-administration observations. Sources: BEA (GDP), BLS (unemployment/CPI), Census (income/poverty), OMB/Treasury/CBO (debt/deficits), CDC (life expectancy), Fed/Saez-Zucman (wealth). Confidence: HIGH where verified in this run; MEDIUM for values reproduced from stable primary series; LOW for early-period (pre-1948) approximations, flagged per field. Presidential periods are NOT treated as causal experiments (root Section 2). Debt/GDP = debt held by the public unless noted. Party: R=Republican, D=Democratic.

administrations.inherited_environment: Antebellum boom (mid-1850s prosperity; escalating slavery-expansion politics)

gdp_avg_growth.note: National accounts reconstructed (Johnston-Williamson/Maddison); Panic of 1857 contraction (1857-58) followed by 1859-60 recovery, then Civil War onset

inflation.note: CPI series begins 1913; antebellum price level roughly stable with 1857-58 deflation

debt_gdp_public.note: Approximate: federal debt ~$29M (1857) rising to ~$90M (1861) on nominal GDP ~$4-4.3B; LOW confidence

major_events: Secession winter 1860-61: 7 states seceded before Lincoln's inauguration
Refused to confront secession; federal property and forts controversy
administrations.verdict_note: Historically rated the WORST US president in scholar surveys for decades (C-SPAN 2021: 44th of 44) before Trump took last place in the 2024 APSA Presidential Greatness Project (Trump 45th, 10.9/100; Buchanan 44th, 16.7). Siena 2022: Johnson 45th, Buchanan 44th, Trump 43rd. Sources: source-031, source-032. IMPORTANT: the ranking reflects secession-crisis inaction (Dred Scott, secession winter), NOT economic performance; 'greatness' polls are subjective scholarly judgment, not economic data. Economy: Panic of 1857 contraction then recovery; all economic figures for this era are LOW-confidence reconstructions.

gdp_avg_growth.note: No official NIPA before 1929; qualitative: rapid early-1900s industrialization growth, periodic panics

inflation.note: Roughly stable prices pre-WWI; CPI series begins 1913

debt_gdp_public.note: Pre-1940 debt data sparse; debt ~low single digits of GDP

major_events: Panic of 1907 → Aldrich-Vreeland 1908, seeds of Fed
administrations.verdict_note: Progressive-era regulation; antitrust; conservation. Economy grew strongly but with repeated financial panics; 1907 panic led to Federal Reserve creation (1913, Wilson).

major_events: Federal Reserve Act 1913 (signed by Wilson, framed under Taft-era debates)
Antitrust: Standard Oil & American Tobacco broken up
administrations.verdict_note: Underrated structural legacy: income tax and Fed groundwork; party split (1912) ended Republican era.

gdp_avg_growth.note: WWI boom 1915-1918; sharp 1920-21 depression (-8.5% est.) at term end

administrations.verdict_note: Created modern fiscal/monetary state; wartime mobilization ended in deep 1920-21 deflationary depression.
Brief; strong recovery from 1921; corruption scandals (Teapot Dome).
Fast growth, low inflation, large tax cuts; seeds of 1929 bubble (leverage, weak regulation) planted here.

gdp_avg_growth.note: Cumulative real GDP fall ~26% 1929-1933; unemployment to ~25%

administrations.verdict_note: Worst economic collapse in US history. Inherited the bubble; policies (tariff, tax increase, gold-standard rigidity, limited intervention) deepened it. Failed re-election.

gdp_avg_growth.note: Massive recovery from depressed base + WWII mobilization; 1933-1944

unemployment.note: 1933 to 1944 (wartime); still 17% in 1939 — recovery was long and incomplete before war

inflation.note: Deflation to 1933, mild 1934-40, WWII price controls then 1946-47 surge

debt_gdp_public.note: Explosion from depression deficits + WWII financing

major_events: New Deal: FDIC, SEC, Social Security 1935, NLRA/Wagner 1935, Fair Labor Standards Act 1938
administrations.verdict_note: Created the modern regulatory/welfare state; deepest recovery in US history but incomplete until war spending; established financial regulation that lasted 50+ years. Four terms; died in office 1945.
Handled demobilization without depression; established Cold War order; debt/GDP fell sharply via growth. Average growth low only because of 1946 arithmetic.

inflation.note: Lowest of any post-WWII administration; 1958-60 mild

debt_gdp_public.note: Gradual decline; balanced budgets except recessions

administrations.verdict_note: Stable, low-inflation growth; three mild recessions; modest fiscal discipline. Middle-class expansion (suburbs, GI Bill cohort) peaks.
Short tenure; strong growth; tax-cut proposal became the Kennedy-Johnson 1964 cut. Assassination cuts causal attribution short.

inflation.note: Rising from 1.3% (1964) to 5.5% (1969) — Great Society + Vietnam overheating

debt_gdp_public.note: Fell despite deficits because growth outpaced debt

administrations.verdict_note: Largest poverty reduction in US history (19%→12.1%); landmark civil rights and health legislation; Vietnam + Great Society spending without full tax financing seeded 1970s inflation.

inflation.note: Rose from 5.5% (1969) to 12.3% (Dec 1974); wage-price controls 1971-73 postponed, then unleashed, inflation

administrations.verdict_note: Environmental legislation legacy; 1971 wage-price freeze distorted markets and arguably worsened inflation; resignation ends term in scandal. Inherited Johnson-era inflation.

unemployment.note: Peak 9.0% (May 1975) — worst since GD at the time

major_events: S&L deregulation seeds (1975 federal preemption rulings)
administrations.verdict_note: Short, crisis-managed tenure; presided over worst recession since 1930s and high inflation; inflation only tamed later by Volcker.

major_events: Deregulation: airlines 1978, trucking 1980, railroads 1980, depository institutions 1980
administrations.verdict_note: Appointed Volcker, whose tightening broke inflation but caused 1980-82 recession — a Democratic appointee delivering Republican-era pain. Deregulation legacy (airlines/trucking) widely judged successful; S&L deregulation seeded 1980s crisis.

unemployment.note: Peak 10.8% (Nov-Dec 1982) — worst since GD; then long decline

debt_gdp_public.note: Debt held by public nearly tripled in $ terms; +$1.9T; largest pre-COVID peacetime debt expansion

administrations.verdict_note: The era-defining conservative administration. Disinflation completed (with Fed credit); growth strong post-1982; stock market +13%/yr. But: tax cuts + defense + rising interest costs tripled public debt as % of GDP (26%→39%) — the modern debt era begins here. S&L deregulation seeds crisis. Inherited inflation crisis; inherited booming 1983-89 expansion was partly recovery from his own 1981-82 recession.

debt_gdp_public.note: Rose due to S&L cleanup + 1990-91 recession + defense cuts not enough

major_events: 1990 Budget Enforcement Act (tax increase + PAYGO; broken 'read my lips' pledge)
Cold War ended (fall of Berlin Wall 1989, USSR dissolution 1991)
North American Free Trade Agreement negotiated
administrations.verdict_note: Recession + S&L cleanup cost him re-election; 1990 tax increase was fiscally responsible but politically fatal; inherited S&L crisis from 1980s deregulation and the 1987 crash aftermath.

debt_gdp_public.note: Largest sustained debt/GDP decline of any post-WWII administration; 4 straight surpluses 1998-2001

crises: Dot-com bubble (inflated 1998-2000; burst after his term)
major_events: 1993 deficit-reduction act (top rate to 39.6%; raised taxes on top 1.2%)
administrations.verdict_note: Best fiscal record of any modern administration (deficits → surpluses); long expansion; stock boom. But: 1999 GLB repeal and dot-com-era leverage are widely cited as contributors to 2008; welfare reform reduced caseloads but is debated on deep-poverty effects. Inherited recovering economy; benefited from productivity boom and tech investment — causes shared with structural forces.

administrations.inherited_environment: Bubble (dot-com peak March 2000; recession began Mar 2001)

debt_gdp_public.note: Rose 20pp: tax cuts + two wars + Medicare Part D + 2001/2007-09 recessions

deficit_avg.note: FY2001 surplus +1.3% → FY2008 -3.2%; FY2009 -9.8% (mostly after term, crisis-driven)

major_events: 2001 & 2003 tax cuts (top rate 39.6%→35%; dividends/cap gains cut; estate tax phase-out)
SEC/HF modernization; subprime deregulation era (2004 net-capital rule)
administrations.verdict_note: Presided over two recessions, the dot-com bust, and the worst financial crisis since 1929. Inherited the dot-com bubble burst and the housing bubble's late buildup (2001-06 low rates, deregulation, and bipartisan housing push). Tax cuts + wars + Part D + crisis tripled debt in $ terms. Stock market: only post-Hoover president with negative cumulative S&P price return. However, 9/11, the housing boom's origins (1990s-2000s), and global credit cycle are external/structural — not purely his.

debt_gdp_public.note: Peak ~79% (2014); rose mostly FY2009-11 (crisis response); roughly flat 2013-2016

deficit_avg.note: FY2009 9.8% (inherited) → FY2016 3.2%; deficit halved and fell every year 2010-2015

major_events: Longest expansion in US history (by end; 2009-2020)
administrations.verdict_note: Inherited the worst crisis since 1929. Stabilized the financial system (TARP/auto rescue arguably prevented depression); ACA insured ~20M; Dodd-Frank constrained banks; stock market +~13.5%/yr from crisis lows (recovery effect). Criticized for slow recovery (real median income didn't surpass 2007 until 2016) and for 2009-11 deficit spike (crisis response). Debt/GDP rose mostly from inherited crisis costs, not ongoing policy; deficits fell to 3.2% by 2016.

administrations.inherited_environment: Mature expansion (oldest recovery on record, 8 yrs)
crises: COVID-19 pandemic & market crash (S&P -34% in 5 weeks, fastest bear market)
major_events: TCJA Dec 2017 (corporate 35%→21%; top individual 39.6%→37%; SALT cap; no CBO score showing self-financing)
Killing of al-Baghdadi; Soleimani strike; Abraham Accords
administrations.verdict_note: Pre-COVID: solid growth (2.7%/yr 2017-19), record-low unemployment, low inflation — continuation of the mature expansion plus TCJA stimulus. TCJA and COVID response (both parties contributed to COVID spending) pushed debt/GDP from 77% to 100%. COVID recession was the sharpest but shortest in history; recovery (pre-vaccine fiscal + monetary + post-vaccine reopening) was fast. Jan 6, 2021 and election denial are major institutional-stability events. Stock market +~13%/yr (recovery from COVID lows).

administrations.inherited_environment: Crisis recovery (COVID recession end; reopening; vaccines rolling out)

debt_gdp_public.note: Roughly flat as % of GDP despite deficits (nominal growth + inflation); FY2024 ~99%

crises: 2023 regional banking crisis (SVB, Signature, First Republic)
major_events: Inflation Reduction Act Aug 2022 (climate + drug pricing; deficit-reducing per CBO)
Dobbs v. Jackson (2022, SCOTUS; abortion access ended in many states)
administrations.verdict_note: Fastest job recovery on record; unemployment at 50-yr lows; real wages rose fastest for lowest earners (2021-24); inflation spiked (global supply shocks + two stimulus rounds + energy war shock; US core peaked ~6.6%, lower than most peers' peaks) then fell to ~2.9% without a recession ('soft landing' per most economists). Deficits fell from 12.4% to 6.4% of GDP. Debt/GDP flat as % despite deficits. Housing affordability deteriorated; life expectancy recovered; immigration surged then was tightened; age and cognitive-aging concerns dominated the final campaign.

administrations.inherited_environment: Expansion with elevated asset valuations and high debt; inflation near target

administrations.verdict_note: INCOMPLETE ADMINISTRATION — treated with the same framework as completed ones but all figures are preliminary or projected. Observed (through Aug 2026): growth positive but decelerating; unemployment low but ticking up; inflation sticky near 3%; deficits ~6% of GDP and rising interest burden ($970B FY2025); stock market at record highs with CAPE ~41 (2nd-highest ever); democracy indices registered sharp declines (V-Dem 0.57, FH 81, EIU 7.65 — lowest on record for each); OBBBA adds ~$3.4T to deficits per CBO. Forecasts: CBO sees debt/GDP 120% by 2036. This period is too early for verdicts on most outcomes.
